Double-Minded
DUB-ul MY-nd
adjective
Greek dipsychos (δίψυχοσ) — from dis (twice, double) + psuche (soul, inner life, mind); the person with two souls, two orientations, two masters. The word appears to be a coinage of James (Jas 1:8; 4:8) with no certain pre-biblical parallels, suggesting that the apostle invented the compound to describe a state of divided spiritual allegiance that Hebrew had no single word to capture. English “double-minded” renders it literally.

Biblical Definition

Double-mindedness is the condition of a person whose inner life is divided between two lords — partly oriented toward God in faith and partly drawn back toward the world in unbelief — resulting in instability across every dimension of life. James identifies the double-minded man as the one who prays with doubt, “like a wave of the sea, driven by the wind and tossed” (Jas 1:6–8), and concludes: “A double minded man is unstable in all his ways.” (Jas 1:8). The instability is total, not partial: divided allegiance corrupts the entire person because it corrupts the heart, which is the governing center of all action.

The Psalmist expressed the opposite commitment in Psalm 119: “SAMECH. I hate vain thoughts: but thy law do I love.” (Ps 119:113). The contrast is stark: wholehearted love for God's law and hatred of the divided soul that claims to love God while holding another allegiance. Christ's teaching in Matthew 6:24 makes the impossibility of double-mindedness structural: “No one can serve two masters” — not that it is merely unwise or inefficient but that it is ontologically impossible; one master will be loved and the other despised, regardless of the double-minded person's intent to serve both.

James issues the remedy in chapter 4: “Cleanse your hands, you sinners — and purify your hearts, you double-minded” (Jas 4:8). Purification of the heart is the cure because double-mindedness is a disorder of the heart, not merely of the will. The Reformed tradition reads this in terms of regeneration and the progressive work of the Spirit who reorients the whole person toward God — so that the increasingly single-minded devotion of the sanctified believer reflects the Spirit's displacement of the divided self.

Origin & Era

Webster (1828) did not define double-minded as a distinct entry; the term is a biblical coinage (James 1:8; 4:8) for the Greek dipsychos — the person of divided soul, unstable in prayer and in all their ways.

expand to see more

DOUBLE-MINDED: not a Webster 1828 entry; a translational rendering of the Greek dipsychos, first appearing in James 1:8 and 4:8.

Dipsychos — from dis (twice) + psuche (soul): a person of two souls, pulled in two directions simultaneously; characterized by instability, wavering prayer, and divided ultimate allegiance.

English “double-minded” has passed into general use from its biblical source to describe any person or institution whose stated commitments and actual motivations are in conflict.

Key Scripture

Jas 1:8 — "A double minded man is unstable in all his ways."

Jas 4:8 — "Draw nigh to God, and he will draw nigh to you. Cleanse your hands, ye sinners; and purify your hearts, ye double minded."

Ps 119:113 — "SAMECH. I hate vain thoughts: but thy law do I love."

Matt 6:24 — "No man can serve two masters: for either he will hate the one, and love the other; or else he will hold to the one, and despise the other. Ye cannot serve God and mammon."

Modern Corruption

Contemporary culture celebrates double-mindedness as intellectual balance, openness to multiple perspectives, or healthy ambiguity — inverting the biblical verdict that a divided soul is unstable and impure, and that purification of the heart requires decisive allegiance to one Lord.

expand to see more

Postmodern epistemology prizes the person who “holds multiple truths in tension” and refuses to commit to a single metanarrative — precisely the posture James names as spiritual pathology. The double-minded person is not morally sophisticated; he is “unstable in all his ways” and his prayers are not heard (Jas 1:6–7). The contemporary celebration of epistemic humility-as-perpetual-undecidedness is the cultural form of the double-mindedness James condemns: it refuses the demanding clarity of a heart cleaved to one Lord, substituting a comfortable ambiguity that costs nothing and changes nothing.

Within evangelical Christianity, double-mindedness often takes the form of seeking God's blessing while maintaining allegiance to competing ultimates — career, reputation, security, comfort — that function as functional lords over the soul. The Puritan diagnosis of the “divided heart” (drawing from Matt 6:24 and Jas 4:1–4) is that worldliness is not primarily behavioral but motivational: the heart that loves the world has made the world its master, however devoutly its owner attends worship. The cure is not mere behavioral adjustment but the heart-renovation that only the Spirit can accomplish — the purification James commands, which the New Covenant promises (Ezek 36:26).

Greek & Hebrew Roots

The Greek dipsychos (two-souled) was coined or repurposed by James to capture the divided orientation of a person pulled between faith and unbelief, God and world.

expand to see more

Greek dis (δίσ) — twice, double; the prefix marking duplication; in dipsychos it names not a healthy complexity but a pathological division — having two souls in the sense of two governing orientations that are mutually incompatible

Greek psuche (ψυχή) — soul, inner life, the animating center of the person; in James's compound, the doubled soul describes a person who lacks the unified inner life that faith produces — a person whose heart is not yet wholehearted toward God

Hebrew leb chalaq — divided heart; the Hebrew equivalent in Psalm 12:2 and Hosea 10:2 (“their heart is divided”); carries the sense of a heart that has been split into portions given to different loyalties, violating the Shema's demand for love with the whole heart, soul, and strength (Deut 6:5)

English double-minded — the King James and subsequent translations' rendering of dipsychos; the compound accurately reproduces the Greek image; it entered English religious vocabulary as a technical term for the spiritually unstable and now appears in general usage for any person of inconsistent, self-contradicting commitments

Usage

"The Puritan Thomas Brooks in Precious Remedies Against Satan's Devices (1652) identified the divided heart as Satan's greatest foothold in the professing Christian — not open apostasy but the gradual seduction of the heart toward multiple masters until prayer becomes hollow and obedience becomes selective; the remedy Brooks prescribes is the regular, deliberate setting of the heart on Christ as the one supreme good."

"The command to “purify your hearts” in James 4:8 uses the adjective hagnos (pure, uncontaminated) and directly addresses the double-minded — connecting heart-purity to single-mindedness and linking both to the drawing-near to God that produces spiritual stability; this sequence (draw near — cleanse — purify) is a compressed description of the whole movement of repentance and faith."

"The Westminster Larger Catechism (Q&A 104) treats the first commandment as requiring “the knowing and acknowledging of God to be the only true God, and our God, and to worship and glorify him accordingly” — which is the positive form of what double-mindedness violates: the complete, undivided acknowledgment of God as the one Lord over every sphere of life."
